extracted.intended_audience: users of PARI/GP (mathematicians and programmers writing GP scripts and functions)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical reference and style rules for writing, debugging, and structuring PARI/GP code, covering variable names, multivariate objects, scoping, user functions, strings/keywords, member functions, and error handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable name syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid name starts with a letter, followed by any number of keyword or alphanumeric characters ([A-Za-z0-9]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Built-in function names and certain constants are reserved and cannot be used; see the built-in list (\c). Names starting with e or E followed by a digit are forbidden for member function names due to floating-point exponent notation; GP names are case sensitive (e.g., i != I, o != O).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserved built-in names
rubrics_metrics.description: The built-in function names and certain constants (e.g., Pi, Euler, Catalan, I, oo) are reserved and cannot be used as variable or member names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempting to use reserved names will produce errors; consult \c or ?.? for lists of reserved identifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on number of variable names
rubrics_metrics.description: GP allows up to 16383 variable names (up to 65535 on 64-bit machines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need thousands of variables, prefer storing values in vectors X[1], X[2], ... rather than creating many named variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of quote operator to register free variables
rubrics_metrics.description: The quote operator 't registers a new free variable t which evaluates to a monomial of degree 1 in that variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because uninitialized variable names are interpreted as quoted variables for backward compatibility, use 't or t = 't explicitly to avoid ambiguous behavior in serious programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on implicit uninitialized-variable behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: For backward compatibility, using a valid variable name for the first time (without assignment) is interpreted as a quoted free variable rather than raising an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This behavior is fragile: if later an assignment t = 1 occurs, programs relying on the earlier free-variable interpretation may break. Use 't or t = 't to be explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assigning to polynomial variables does not retroactively change earlier expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assigning a value to a polynomial variable does not affect previous expressions that referenced it; those expressions must be re-evaluated with eval to see the new value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: creating an expression involving 't, then setting t=2, requires eval(%expr) to obtain the numeric result. Use eval when you need to take new bindings into account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quote in subst when substituting quoted/free variables
rubrics_metrics.description: When substituting into expressions that used quoted variables, use the quoted identifier in subst, e.g. subst(p, 't, 3), otherwise gp may expect a variable name and error out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids errors where gp expects a variable name at top-level because the variable has become bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit variable priority (ordering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Variables are implicitly ordered by the interpreter: when a new identifier is input, it is registered with strictly lower priority than any variable already in use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The internal multivariate representation treats the highest-priority variable as the main variable; check ordering with variable(). To control ordering, declare variables in the desired order before computations or read a variables.gp file; use varhigher/varlower to create variables with specific priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predefine variables to control multivariate ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want a specific internal ordering of variables, define them in the desired sequence in a gp session or in an initialization file (e.g. 'x; 'y; 'z; ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no way to change the priority of existing variables, but you can create new variables with varhigher/varlower. Consistent ordering across sessions can be obtained by reading a variables.gp file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of variable ordering when performing Euclidean division
rubrics_metrics.description: PARI assumes divisions of multivariate polynomials take place in the fraction field of the coefficient ring, which depends on the implicit main variable determined by variable ordering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This affects results of operators like % and /, and functions like numerator, denominator, and content; unexpected invertibility or null rings can occur when the coefficient ring makes a variable invertible. Consider using divrem(x,y,var) when you need explicit control of the main variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multivariate power series are single-variable objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Power series in PARI are fundamentally single-variable objects; PARI cannot handle multivariate error terms like O(x^i y^j).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat power series carefully: if x has higher priority than y, then y is treated as not depending on x; substitution of expressions involving higher-priority variables into lower-priority variables is forbidden or leads to incorrect results. The implementation cannot represent an error term like O(x*z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid substituting expressions that violate variable-priority rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting an expression involving high-priority variables into a low-priority variable can produce incorrect or inconsistent error terms in power series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the rule that variables with higher priority are assumed independent of lower-priority ones; if you must substitute such expressions, be aware of the possible spurious terms and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope definitions and distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: A scope is an enclosing context where names and values are attached; GP implements both lexical (static) scoping with my and dynamic scoping with local.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use my for lexical scoping (value private to block determined at compile time) and local for dynamic scoping (push/pop value stack). The argument of eval is evaluated in the enclosing scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer lexical scoping (my) for private variables
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice you almost certainly want true private variables and should use my almost exclusively rather than local.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local (dynamic) variables act like temporary values visible to called subroutines; they can lead to non-obvious dependencies on calling context. Explicitly scope variables to the smallest possible block.

rubrics_metrics.name: Named parameters and loop indices are lexically scoped
rubrics_metrics.description: Named parameters in function definitions and loop indices used by iterative constructs (for, prod, sum, vector, matrix, plot, etc.) have lexical scope within the function or construct body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loop indices and named parameters are initialized and restored upon exit; if you break out of loops, the loop index is restored to its previous value (so do not expect it to retain the last iterated value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on loop index after premature exit (break)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you exit a loop prematurely with break, the loop index value is restored to its prior value and will not reflect the last iterated value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workarounds: save the loop index into another variable before breaking, or wrap the loop in a user function and use return instead of break to obtain the iterated index.

rubrics_metrics.name: my/local declaration behavior and default initialization
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of variables can be lexically or dynamically scoped with my or local; variables without explicit default values in the declaration are initialized to 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want them initialized as free variables use quoting: my(x = 'x, y = 'y). Declarations can include initial values and can be placed anywhere within a function body to restrict scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: eval evaluates in the given (enclosing) scope
rubrics_metrics.description: eval is evaluated in the enclosing scope and can access values of lexical variables in that scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: x = 1; my(x = 0); eval("x") yields 0 as eval sees the local x scoped to that command line.

rubrics_metrics.name: User-defined functions are GP objects and scoped like variables
rubrics_metrics.description: User-defined functions are ordinary GP objects bound to variables; they follow the same scoping rules as other objects and can be lexically scoped where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defining helper functions lexically to the block where they are needed yields cleaner code than defining everything in global scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function definition syntaxes and printing behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions can be defined as (list) -> seq or f(list) = seq; a trailing semicolon suppresses printing of the function object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you omit the semicolon, GP prints the function object; parentheses around bodies and variants with braces are available for clearer multi-line functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments are passed by value (copy-on-write)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments passed to functions are assigned copies of actual parameters; a form of copy-on-write avoids duplication until modification occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modifying a function's argument inside the function does not change the caller's variable. Formal parameters are lexically scoped to the function body and parameter names must be distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: No duplicate formal parameter names allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not allowed to use the same variable name for different parameters of your function (e.g., f(x,x) = 1 is an error).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GP will report 'variable declared twice' for duplicate parameter names; ensure parameter lists contain distinct identifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variadic (unlimited-argument) functions syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: To define a function taking an unlimited number of arguments, use syntax (list_of_formals, var[..]) -> seq, where var becomes a vector of remaining arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: f(c[..]) = sum(i=1,#c,c[i]); sep(s,v[..]) = for(...) ; use the var parameter to iterate over extra args.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide explicit default argument values and use strictargs
rubrics_metrics.description: The implicit default value for uninitialized formal parameters is 0 (deprecated); the recommended practice is to explicitly set defaults using =expr in the definition, and enable default(strictargs,1) to make arguments mandatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When strictargs is set, missing mandatory arguments raise an error. Use explicit defaults to avoid surprising results and allow empty-argument trick f(6,,1) to skip intermediate defaults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use addhelp to attach help messages to functions
rubrics_metrics.description: You can add a specific help message for your function using addhelp; by default ?name prints the function definition and defaults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The online help system also handles user-defined help, but addhelp allows custom descriptive text for your functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of shadowing and nested-scope pitfalls (forprime example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Loop constructs may introduce their own lexically-scoped variables which can shadow outer variables with the same name, causing surprising results (e.g., returning 0 instead of the found prime).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pre-declaring the same name both outside and inside a loop; either return directly from the loop (return(p)) or use distinct variable names to prevent shadowing and logic errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursion depth limited by OS stack
rubrics_metrics.description: The operating system limits recursion depth for GP; deep recursive calls will raise a 'deep recursion' error and there is no way to increase this limit from within gp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To increase recursion limits before launching gp, raise the process stack size using shell tools (ulimit, limit) appropriate to your shell/OS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions as first-class objects and higher-order usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions can be passed as parameters, returned from functions, stored in arrays, and applied programmatically (e.g., calc(f,x) = f(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use anonymous functions when a function is not needed elsewhere (e.g., calc(x->x^2,3)). APPLY(f,v) pattern applies a function to every vector element; built-in apply is more general and can handle lists/matrices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closures capture copies, not live mutable contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: GP closures incorporate the defining context but access a copy of lexical variables, so modifying the captured variable inside the closure does not change the original context for future calls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closures cannot simulate true mutable objects with private state across calls; example shows incrementing within closure does not persist as expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Member function syntax and restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Member functions use dot notation structure.member and are defined with var.member = seq where var is scoped to seq; built-in member functions are read-only and cannot be redefined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Member functions are often simple accessors (x.a = x[1]) and their namespace is independent from variables/functions, allowing short names without clashes. To avoid performance issues, do not call expensive member functions repeatedly on constant objects in tight loops—store the value first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Member function naming rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid member function name starts with a letter followed by keyword or alphanumeric characters; built-in member names are reserved and cannot be used; names starting with e/E followed by a digit are forbidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempting to redefine built-in member functions will produce an error; use a different name (e.g., x.myj) if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: String literal syntax and escape sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Strings are enclosed in double quotes "..."; whitespace inside strings is significant; escape sequences: \e = Escape, \n = Newline, \t = Tab; \x expands to x for any other character (so \" is required to produce a double-quote inside a string).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automatic concatenation: placing two string literals adjacent concatenates them. Be careful: "a"[1] is invalid since string is not a GP object with components; outside string context expansions will behave differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: String expansion and automatic conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: In string context, any inserted expression is evaluated and converted to a string (expansion) before concatenation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "a" 1+1 "b" becomes "a2b". If a symbol was never assigned previously, its expansion yields the printed monomial, which may accidentally produce the expected literal. Beware largest-possible-expression evaluation in string context causing unexpected parsing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keywords vs Strings
rubrics_metrics.description: Keywords are special relatives of strings automatically assumed quoted (no expansion), while strings are expanded; both can be concatenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In keyword context expansion is never performed: typing a b+b in keyword context yields the literal 'ab+b'. GP functions declare argument prototypes that specify whether they expect GEN, string, keyword, or unevaluated sequences—only a small set of keyword words are meaningful for a given function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Which functions process arguments in string or keyword context
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain functions/processors expect string or keyword contexts; e.g., Str, addhelp(second arg), default(second arg), error, extern, plotstring(second arg), plotterm(first arg), read/readvec, system, all printxxx/writexxx functions use string context; alias, default(first arg), install(all but last), trap(first arg), whatnow use keyword context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the reference list when writing code that relies on string vs keyword behavior to ensure correct expansion/quoting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error types and recover option
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of errors: syntax errors (compiler) and runtime errors (PARI library or evaluator). Both are fatal to the current computation; by default gp returns to the prompt, but setting recover off makes gp exit immediately on untrapped errors (useful for batch mode).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the recover option (Sec. 3.4.37) to control whether gp should exit on untrapped errors during batch runs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error messages include context and caret to indicate location
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting syntax errors gp prints part of the input expression and indicates where the error occurred with a caret or arrow, providing meaningful context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Error messages may seem cryptic because the parser cannot know programmer intent; read the caret-marked context to diagnose missing tokens (parentheses, commas) or unexpected tokens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Runtime errors often reveal typos or undefined names
rubrics_metrics.description: Runtime errors from evaluation can indicate that a function or symbol is undefined (e.g., siN is a typo for sin) and are reported with a contextual message showing where the error occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish syntax/compiler errors from runtime/library errors; runtime library errors tend to be more mathematical and informative (e.g., Mod/1 over a coset null ring). Use the provided context to debug typos and incorrect types.
